nameStory: The blacksaddle pelt lichen gets its name from its distinctive reproductive structures that look like tiny black saddles perched on the lichen's surface. These unique tubular apothecia (spore-producing structures) also resemble painted fingernails, giving this species its unmistakable appearance. Like other pelt lichens, it has a leathery, skin-like texture that feels soft and flexible when moist.
description: Blacksaddle pelt lichen is a foliose (leaf-like) lichen that grows flat against its surface in overlapping, pelt-like lobes. This uncommon New England species belongs to a large family of pelt lichens, all of which have a distinctive leathery texture and grow in rosette or spreading patterns. What makes this species truly special are its black, tubular reproductive structures that look like tiny saddles sitting on top of the lichen. When you find one, you'll likely remember it forever because of these unmistakable black "saddles" that no other lichen quite matches.

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Look for unique black, tubular apothecia that resemble tiny saddles or painted fingernails sitting on the lichen surface - no other pelt lichen has quite this shape

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Foliose (leaf-like) with overlapping lobes that spread outward in a rosette or irregular pattern, lying flat against the substrate

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels leathery and pliable when moist, like soft leather or suede, becoming more papery when completely dry

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Upper surface typically grayish to brownish, may appear more vibrant when wet, contrasting sharply with the distinctive black reproductive structures

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual lobes several centimeters across, with the entire lichen potentially spreading to cover a hand-sized area or larger over many years

habitat: Based on its extreme rarity in New England (only one recorded observation), blacksaddle pelt lichen likely grows on soil, moss, or decaying organic matter in moist, shaded environments. Like other pelt lichens, it probably prefers areas with consistent moisture and protection from direct sunlight, possibly in rich woodlands or along stream banks. Given its scarcity, it may require very specific microhabitat conditions that are uncommon in our region.

seasonality.spring: As moisture returns to the forest, the lichen becomes more pliable and vibrant in color, making it easier to spot against the brown leaf litter. Black saddle-like structures become more prominent.
seasonality.summer: During humid periods, the lichen maintains its leathery texture and the black apothecia are most visible and well-developed. May be harder to spot during very dry spells when it becomes more cryptic.
seasonality.fall: Excellent time for detection as fallen leaves create moist conditions and the distinctive black saddle structures stand out against autumn colors. The lichen remains active in cool, damp weather.
seasonality.winter: Still visible and identifiable under snow-free conditions, especially during winter thaws when moisture brings out the leathery texture and makes the black reproductive structures more obvious.

funFact: This lichen is so rare in New England that it has been documented only once in the entire region, making it one of our most elusive species - finding one would be like discovering a botanical unicorn in your own backyard!
confusionNotes: The tubular, saddle-shaped black apothecia make this species nearly impossible to confuse with other lichens once you know what to look for. Other pelt lichens may have dark reproductive structures, but none have quite this distinctive saddle or fingernail shape - think "black saddles on a leather couch" as your memory trick.
contextualKnowledge: With only one observation recorded in all of New England, this species represents the incredible diversity hidden within the lichen world - there may be many more rare species waiting to be discovered by careful observers. Its scarcity doesn't necessarily mean it's endangered; it might simply prefer microhabitats that botanists haven't thoroughly explored yet.
compareHints: Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface. While freckled pelt lichen has white spots scattered across its surface, blacksaddle pelt lacks these "freckles" and is identified primarily by its unique black saddle structures. The saddle-shaped apothecia are truly diagnostic - no other pelt lichen in New England has this particular feature.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.
Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees.

Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen.
Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface.

Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
